Low Back Pain in an Adult

red flags and when to image · acute pain with no red flags · inflammatory back pain and spondyloarthritisIs there a red flag or a neurologic deficit, and does the pain improve when the patient moves?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Acute low back pain, no red flag, normal neurologic exam: no imaging; an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or acetaminophen, and stay active Why no imagingDisc herniations and bulges are common in people without symptoms, so an early scan mostly finds lesions unrelated to the pain; up to 85% of patients recover without surgery within 6 weeks whatever the cause.
  • A history of cancer, fever or injection drug use, or a bladder or saddle change, means imaging even when the neurologic exam is normal
  • Night pain that eases on getting up is inflammatory; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves, with a cancer history or weight loss, points to malignancy
What it is

Usually mechanical; a few cases are infection, inflammation, cancer or fracture

Sort by

Red flags and the neurologic exam, then how the pain answers rest and movement

Hands off

A fragility fracture: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment; anterior uveitis: The Red Eye; buttock pain from the hip or piriformis: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

2Urgent risks
Cauda equina syndromeUrinary retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, sciatica on one side or both, lost anal tone and ankle reflexes

If the bladder or the saddle is involved, choose emergent MRI and surgical decompression.

Spinal cord compressionUpper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia (reflexes may be low at first when the onset is acute), an extensor plantar response, a sensory level

If cancer is known or suspected, choose dexamethasone first, then emergent MRI of the whole spine.

Spinal epidural abscessFever, focal spinal tenderness and neurologic signs after injection drug use or bacteremia

If fever comes with a neurologic sign, choose MRI and blood cultures.

Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysmOlder smoker; sudden back pain with syncope or hypotension; a pulsatile mass

If the patient is unstable, choose straight to surgery.

3Differential
Low back pain, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Lumbosacral strainAfter lifting; paraspinal tenderness; a symmetric, belt-like acheAcute, settles within weeks; normal neurologic exam, negative straight-leg raise
Lumbar radiculopathy from a discPain shooting below the knee; positive straight-leg raiseSudden onset; most settle within 6 weeks; imaging (MRI) for a deficit or pain past 6 weeks (the ladder, rung 2)
Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)Older; buttock and leg pain on walking or standingChronic; eased by sitting or leaning forward (shopping cart, uphill, cycling); pulses normal, unlike vascular claudication
Ankylosing spondylitis The familySeronegative spondyloarthritis (PAIR: psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, reactive arthritis, formerly Reiter syndrome) shares human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27), enthesitis and anterior uveitis. Ankylosing spondylitis also brings aortic regurgitation (aortitis), stiffens the chest wall (restrictive lung disease), may scar the upper lobes, and thins bone. Its mimic, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, affects an older man with flowing ossification over 4 or more vertebrae and normal sacroiliac joints; it is not spondyloarthritis.Man, most often aged 20 to 40; morning stiffness that eases with use; night painInsidious, over 3 months; sacroiliitis on imaging
Vertebral metastasis RouteProstate cancer reaches the lumbar spine through the vertebral (Batson) venous plexus, often as osteoblastic lesions.Prior cancer (prostate, breast, kidney, thyroid, lung); weight lossWeeks, worsening; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves; MRI with contrast
Vertebral osteomyelitisInjection drug use, hemodialysis or bacteremia; focal tendernessContinuous pain; fever often absent; ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) high; MRI
Vertebral compression fractureOlder, osteoporosis or chronic glucocorticoids; a minor fall or liftSudden; point tenderness over one vertebra; radiograph first
Inflammatory versus mechanical back pain
FeatureInflammatoryMechanical
OnsetBy age 40, gradual, over 3 monthsAny age, often sudden after an event
NightWakes the patient; eases on getting upUsually absent
Morning stiffnessMarked, eases with useBrief
Rest and activityWorse with rest, better with exerciseBetter with rest
4Workup
Acute low back pain: start on the lowest rung not yet tried
RungDoMove on when
1An NSAID or acetaminophen; stay active; a nonbenzodiazepine muscle relaxant second lineStill painful at 4 to 6 weeks, or a new red flag
2Physical therapy and exerciseRadicular pain past 6 weeks: MRI
3Epidural glucocorticoid injection, severe or persistent radicular painConservative care fails
4Surgical referralCauda equina, or an unequivocal disc herniation with a progressive deficit or intractable pain after 6 weeks
Treatment by cause
CauseTreatment
Ankylosing spondylitisAn NSAID and daily exercise, then a TNF (tumor necrosis factor) or IL-17 (interleukin-17) inhibitor Second lineMethotrexate and sulfasalazine help only peripheral arthritis. Blocking TNF impairs granulomas and can reactivate latent tuberculosis.
Malignant spinal cord compressionDexamethasone, then decompression, or radiation for a radiosensitive tumor
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Foot drop or trouble heel-walkingL4 to L5 disc on the L5 rootA motor deficit: MRI promptly
Young man, back pain, cough and lung nodulesTesticular cancerScrotal ultrasound and tumor markers
Fused (bamboo) spine, new pain after a minor fallFracture of the rigid spineImage for a fracture
Diarrhea or urethritis, then knee and ankle arthritis and red eyesReactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome)Diagnose it clinically from the history and exam; the joint fluid is sterile
Ankylosing spondylitis with a painful red eye and photophobiaAnterior uveitis, its most common complication outside the jointsFollow the red-eye workup

Pause point. The bait: imaging every back pain, or calling cancer pain mechanical because the neurologic exam is normal. Read the history first, then image by cause.

Practice
  1. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of low back pain now pain down both legs cannot pass urine since this morning Numb over the buttocks and inner thighs Afebrile · bladder scan 800 mL · anal tone reduced → Emergent MRI + decompression → urinary retention and saddle anesthesia are cauda equina syndrome: emergent MRI and decompression
  2. 40-year-old man has 1 week of low back pain began 1 day after moving furniture tender over the paraspinal muscles, not the spine No fever, chills, constipation or urinary incontinence Afebrile · reflexes, strength and sensation normal → No imaging → acute pain with a mechanical cause and a history full of pertinent negatives needs no imaging: an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and stay active
  3. 62-year-old woman has 6 weeks of low back pain treated for breast cancer 4 years ago worse at night, not relieved by rest Neurologic exam normal Afebrile · no weight loss → MRI for metastasis → prior cancer with night pain needs MRI with contrast even with a normal neurologic exam
  4. 72-year-old woman on chronic prednisone has sudden back pain began after a minor fall point tenderness over one midline lumbar vertebra No leg pain, numbness or weakness Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Vertebral compression fracture → age over 70, chronic steroids and a minor fall point to a vertebral compression fracture: lumbar radiograph first
  5. 47-year-old woman has 5 days of low back pain after gardening chronic kidney disease, stage 3 bleeding gastric ulcer last year No fever, weight loss or bladder change Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL · neurologic exam normal → Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID → same tier, a different agent: kidney disease and a prior bleed rule out an oral NSAID, so acetaminophen or a topical NSAID
  6. 47-year-old woman has 3 weeks of low back and left leg pain now cannot lift the front of her left foot foot slaps on walking No bladder or bowel change Afebrile · left ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 · saddle sensation normal → Urgent MRI → a new foot drop is a progressive deficit: urgent MRI, without the bladder or saddle signs that make it an emergency
  7. 55-year-old woman has 2 months of back pain that wakes her at night not relieved by getting up and moving lost 6 kg without trying Treated for breast cancer 3 years ago Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Metastasis → night pain unrelieved by moving, with prior cancer and weight loss, is metastasis, not inflammatory back pain: MRI
  8. 34-year-old man who injects drugs has 1 week of back pain fever and chills focal tenderness over one lumbar spinous process No leg weakness T 38.9 °C · erythrocyte sedimentation rate 98 mm/h → Vertebral osteomyelitis → fever with focal spinal tenderness in injection drug use is vertebral osteomyelitis: MRI with contrast plus blood cultures
  9. 47-year-old woman has 8 weeks of low back pain pain shoots down the lateral leg to the top of the foot no better with an NSAID No bladder change Afebrile · strength normal · left straight-leg raise positive → MRI, PT, consider epidural → radicular symptoms past 6 weeks: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and physical therapy (PT), with an epidural steroid injection if conservative care keeps failing
  10. 72-year-old man has 1 hour of sudden severe back pain pulsatile, tender mass above the umbilicus pale and light-headed Smoker with peripheral arterial disease and hypertension BP 82/50 mm Hg · HR 124/min → Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm → back pain with a pulsatile mass and hypotension is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: straight to surgery; do not delay for CT
  11. 68-year-old man has 1 year of buttock and leg pain when walking relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping cart cycles without pain No back pain at rest Afebrile · pedal pulses normal · strength normal → Spinal stenosis → leg pain on walking relieved by flexing forward, with normal pulses, is spinal stenosis
  12. 38-year-old man has 2 weeks of low back pain pain shoots below the right knee into the foot right straight-leg raise positive Began while lifting a sofa Afebrile · strength normal → Radiculopathy → pain radiating below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise is radiculopathy
  13. 34-year-old man has 4 months of low back pain better with activity, worse with rest morning stiffness over 30 minutes Wakes in the second half of the night Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Inflammatory back pain → under 40, over 3 months, better with movement: inflammatory back pain; sacroiliac joint radiographs, with HLA-B27 supportive only
  14. 26-year-old man has 6 months of low back pain improves with exercise, worse after sitting morning stiffness for an hour Sacroiliac joint radiographs are normal Afebrile · reduced Schober test · chest expansion reduced → MRI of the SI joints → radiographs normal with suspicion still high: MRI of the sacroiliac joints shows active sacroiliitis first; HLA-B27 is supportive only
  15. 30-year-old man with HLA-B27-positive sacroiliitis has a red, painful left eye began yesterday photophobia and blurred vision No discharge or itching Afebrile · small left pupil · redness greatest around the cornea → Anterior uveitis → the eye complication of spondyloarthritis is anterior uveitis: topical steroid and a cycloplegic
  16. 45-year-old man with a fused, bamboo-like spine for 15 years new exertional dyspnea diastolic murmur at the left sternal border No chest pain or syncope BP 150/50 mm Hg · HR 76/min → Aortic regurgitation from aortitis → aortitis widens the aortic root: aortic regurgitation
  17. 52-year-old man with HLA-B27-positive sacroiliitis for 20 years new neck pain after a minor fall pain on any neck movement Old radiographs show a fused spine Afebrile · strength and sensation normal → Spinal fracture → a rigid spine is brittle: fracture after minor trauma, so CT (computed tomography) of the spine
  18. 24-year-old man has 1 week of a swollen right knee and left ankle bloody diarrhea 2 weeks ago red eyes and burning on urination No rash or nail changes T 37.8 °C · rheumatoid factor negative → Reactive arthritis → asymmetric lower-limb arthritis weeks after dysentery, with conjunctivitis and urethritis, is reactive arthritis
  19. 68-year-old man with diabetes has back stiffness radiograph: flowing ossification along the front of 4 or more vertebrae sacroiliac joints normal No morning stiffness over 30 minutes Afebrile · HLA-B27 negative → Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis → flowing anterior ossification with spared sacroiliac joints in an older man with diabetes is diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not spondyloarthritis
Common wrong answers Bed rest: harmful, delays recovery. CT of the lumbosacral spine: not indicated at 1 week, and MRI is the modality for disc and nerve root. Epidural injection: only after 4 to 6 weeks of failed conservative care. Oral prednisone: does not improve acute sciatica.
Transferable rule

When most patients do not need a test, ask whether this patient is the exception. A dense list of pertinent negatives supports doing less. When a symptom fits two categories, its behavior separates them: here, what happens when the patient gets up.
